words.shortDefinition: Alistair Cockburn's 2005 pattern that isolates domain logic from delivery mechanisms via explicit port interfaces.
words.simpleDefinition: Hexagonal architecture places your domain at the center, surrounded by named interfaces called ports. Every external technology — the web framework, the database, the email sender — connects through those ports, never directly to the domain. The result is a core that can be tested without any infrastructure and swapped between delivery mechanisms freely.
words.longDefinition: Published by Alistair Cockburn in 2005, hexagonal architecture (also called Ports and Adapters) solved the persistent problem of business logic entangled with delivery mechanisms. The traditional layered stack placed presentation at the top, business logic in the middle, and data access at the bottom — which meant that testing a single if-statement required a running web server and a live database. Cockburn's solution was a two-zone model: an inside (the domain and its use cases) and an outside (everything the application talks to). The boundary between inside and outside is enforced by explicit, named interfaces. The hexagonal shape of the diagram was chosen not because six sides are significant but because it conveniently shows multiple entry points around a perimeter without implying a top-down hierarchy. In a DDD context, hexagonal architecture is the default structural pattern for keeping aggregates, entities, and domain services free of framework contamination.
words.connector: Think of hexagonal architecture like a smartphone and its ports: the phone's core functions don't care whether you plug in USB-C headphones, a Lightning adapter, or a wireless dongle — the port is the contract, and any technology that satisfies it plugs in.
words.techContext: After adopting hexagonal architecture, our team could run the entire domain test suite in 400 ms with no database or HTTP server — the ports replaced all infrastructure with in-memory stubs.
words.exampleSentence: Switching from REST to gRPC took one afternoon because hexagonal architecture confined all HTTP concerns to a single driving adapter that called the unchanged primary ports.
words.etymology: Named by Alistair Cockburn in his 2005 paper; the hexagon shape was chosen to suggest multiple symmetric entry points rather than the top-down hierarchy of a rectangle.

words.shortDefinition: The implementation of hexagonal architecture: ports are interfaces the domain defines; adapters are technology-specific implementations.
words.simpleDefinition: A port is a named interface written in the domain's vocabulary — OrderRepository, PaymentGateway, NotificationService — with no mention of any technology. An adapter is a concrete class that implements the port using a specific technology: PostgresOrderRepository, StripePaymentGateway, SendGridNotificationService. The domain depends only on ports; adapters depend on the port definition and implement the real wiring.
words.longDefinition: Ports and Adapters is the formal name Alistair Cockburn gave to hexagonal architecture. The term pair is more precise than the nickname: a port is a seam on the boundary of the application. It is the point at which the application's internal world ends and external technology begins. Ports come in two directions — primary (or driving) ports that expose what the application can do, such as use-case interfaces that HTTP controllers call, and secondary (or driven) ports that declare what the application needs from outside, such as repository interfaces that database adapters implement. Adapters are interchangeable by design; swapping a Kafka adapter for a RabbitMQ adapter never touches the domain. In DDD projects, the discipline of keeping interfaces in the domain or application package — not the infrastructure package — is what enforces the Dependency Inversion Principle at architectural scale.
words.connector: Think of ports as the standard plug shapes on a power strip and adapters as the country-specific plugs. The strip defines the contract; any plug that fits works. The appliance (domain) never touches the wall socket (infrastructure) directly.
words.techContext: Our secondary port EventPublisher is a three-line interface in the domain package; the KafkaEventPublisher adapter in the infrastructure package implements it. Swapping to RabbitMQ required touching only the adapter.
words.exampleSentence: By placing the EventPublisher port in the domain module, we could test every aggregate event emission with a simple in-memory adapter before the Kafka cluster was even provisioned.
words.etymology: From Cockburn's 2005 paper; 'port' borrowed from hardware I/O ports — a standardized socket that accepts any compliant connector.

words.shortDefinition: A driving interface the application exposes (REST endpoint, CLI, message consumer) that initiates use cases.
words.simpleDefinition: A primary port is the application's front door — a use-case interface the domain defines that describes what the application can do. HTTP controllers, CLI command handlers, Kafka message consumers, and test classes are all driving adapters that call a primary port. The port knows nothing about HTTP or Kafka; the adapters handle the protocol while delegating the decision to the port.
words.longDefinition: In hexagonal architecture, primary ports (also called inbound or driving ports) sit on the left side of the hexagonal diagram. They expose the application's capabilities as named, technology-neutral interfaces. For example, a PlaceOrderUseCase interface with a single placeOrder(PlaceOrderCommand) method is a primary port. Multiple adapters can call the same primary port: an HTTP REST controller, a gRPC service handler, a CLI command parser, a Kafka message listener, and a unit test class can all call placeOrder() without the application core knowing or caring which delivery mechanism was used. This makes the use case reusable across delivery channels. In DDD teams, primary ports often map one-to-one with bounded-context application service methods, each representing a discrete use case in the ubiquitous language.
words.connector: Think of a primary port like a TV's remote control API — the physical remote, a smart-home app, and a voice assistant are all different adapters, but they all call the same 'change channel' interface the TV exposes.
words.techContext: Our PlaceOrderUseCase primary port is called by three driving adapters: the REST controller in production, a CLI tool for support operations, and a test stub in the unit test suite — the application service implementation is identical for all three.
words.exampleSentence: Adding a gRPC interface required only a new driving adapter that translated Protobuf messages into PlaceOrderCommand objects and called the existing primary port — the domain was unchanged.
words.etymology: 'Primary' signals it is the initiating (driving) side — the entry point that starts the interaction, as opposed to secondary ports which the application calls out to.

words.shortDefinition: A driven interface the domain defines for infrastructure it needs (database, email, payment) that adapters implement.
words.simpleDefinition: A secondary port is the application saying 'I need something from outside — here is the interface it must satisfy.' The application core calls the interface; it never calls PostgreSQL, Kafka, or SendGrid directly. Those are driven adapters that implement the secondary port. Repositories, event publishers, notification services, and payment gateways are all common secondary ports in a DDD application.
words.longDefinition: Secondary ports (also called outbound or driven ports) sit on the right side of the hexagonal diagram. They represent dependencies the application core has on the outside world, expressed as interfaces that live in the domain or application layer — never in the infrastructure layer. This placement is the key discipline: if OrderRepository were defined in the infrastructure package, the domain would have to import infrastructure to compile, which inverts the inversion. Common secondary ports in DDD: OrderRepository (persisting and retrieving aggregates), EventPublisher (dispatching domain events to a broker), NotificationService (sending email or push), PaymentGateway (charging a payment method), and Clock (abstracting system time for deterministic testing). Driven adapters — PostgresOrderRepository, KafkaEventPublisher, StripePaymentGateway — implement these ports and live in the infrastructure layer, where all technology-specific code belongs.
words.connector: Think of a secondary port like a job description the company (domain) writes: 'We need someone who can store and retrieve orders.' The recruiting agency (infrastructure) finds a candidate (PostgreSQL adapter) who matches the description.
words.techContext: Our Clock secondary port allowed us to inject a fixed-time stub in tests, making every date-sensitive invariant in the Order aggregate deterministically verifiable without freezing the system clock.
words.exampleSentence: Because NotificationService was a secondary port owned by the domain, we swapped our email provider from Mailgun to SendGrid in a single adapter class with no changes to any aggregate or application service.
words.etymology: 'Secondary' signals it is the driven (responding) side — the application calls out to it rather than it calling in, making it secondary to the primary direction of flow.

words.shortDefinition: The architectural rule that source code dependencies must always point inward, toward the domain, never outward to infrastructure.
words.simpleDefinition: The dependency rule is a single constraint: nothing in the inner rings (domain, application) may import anything from the outer rings (infrastructure, frameworks). Domain entities never import @Entity annotations. Domain services never import HTTP request types. Use case interactors never import database driver classes. This one constraint is what makes the domain portable, testable without infrastructure, and free to outlast any framework choice.
words.longDefinition: The dependency rule appears in Robert C. Martin's Clean Architecture (2017), but the principle underlies hexagonal and onion architecture equally. It states that source-code dependencies may only point inward — toward the domain — and never outward toward infrastructure. In practical terms: the domain/application packages may import from each other but not from the infrastructure package. The infrastructure package imports from both. This is mechanically enforceable: in Java, ArchUnit lets teams write an architecture test that fails the build if any class in the domain package has a compile-time import from the infrastructure package. In Python, import-linter enforces the same. In Go, Go modules make it structural. The dependency rule is the boundary between 'architecture in documentation' and 'architecture that survives contact with a deadline.' Without enforcement tooling, violations accumulate silently; with tooling, they become compiler errors.
words.connector: Think of the dependency rule like a one-way turnstile at a museum: visitors (adapters) can enter the gallery (domain) to see the art, but the paintings (domain code) never leave the gallery to visit the gift shop (infrastructure).
words.techContext: We added an ArchUnit test to the build that fails if any class in com.example.ordering.domain has an import from com.example.ordering.infrastructure — two violations were caught in code review before they merged.
words.exampleSentence: The dependency rule violation showed up as a build failure the moment a developer imported a JPA annotation into an aggregate class, keeping the domain clean without relying on code review vigilance.
words.etymology: Popularized by Robert C. Martin in 'Clean Architecture' (2017); the 'rule' framing emphasizes it is a constraint to be enforced, not a guideline to aspire to.

words.shortDefinition: Jeffrey Palermo's layered variant of hexagonal architecture where the domain model sits at the center with all dependencies pointing inward.
words.simpleDefinition: Onion architecture names the concentric rings explicitly: Domain Model at the center, then Domain Services, then Application Services, then Infrastructure at the outermost layer. Every ring may only import from rings closer to the center. This is the same dependency rule as hexagonal architecture, but with more granular ring names that matter when the domain is large enough that the boundary between domain model and application services becomes important.
words.longDefinition: Jeffrey Palermo published Onion Architecture on his blog in 2008. Where Cockburn's hexagonal architecture described two zones — inside and outside — Palermo named four concentric rings. The Domain Model ring contains aggregates, entities, value objects, and domain events: pure logic with no dependencies on anything else. The Domain Services ring contains operations that span multiple aggregates. The Application Services ring contains use case orchestrators that coordinate domain objects and call secondary ports. The Infrastructure ring is outermost: adapters for persistence, messaging, HTTP, and driving adapters that initiate the flow. The name comes from the visual: slice through the architecture and you see concentric layers, like an onion cross-section. The practical contribution over hexagonal architecture is naming the inner rings, which provides vocabulary for conversations about where to place logic that spans entities but does not quite belong on any single one.
words.connector: Think of onion architecture like the layers of an onion: the core (domain model) has no outer layer coating it, each successive layer wraps the ones inside, and the outermost skin (infrastructure) touches the environment — but you peel outward, never drill inward.
words.techContext: When a DDD service dispute arose over whether a cross-aggregate operation belonged in a domain service or an application service, onion architecture's explicit ring names gave us precise vocabulary to resolve it.
words.exampleSentence: Onion architecture's explicit Domain Services ring resolved a year-long debate about where to place our pricing calculator — it coordinated three aggregates but contained genuine business rules, placing it clearly inside the domain boundary.
words.etymology: Named by Jeffrey Palermo in 2008; the onion metaphor was chosen for the visual of concentric rings that form a coherent whole — peel an onion and you see nested layers, each containing the one inside it.

words.shortDefinition: Robert Martin's architecture organizing code into concentric rings (entities, use cases, adapters, frameworks) with the dependency rule enforced.
words.simpleDefinition: Clean Architecture is Robert C. Martin's synthesis of hexagonal and onion architecture into four named rings and universal vocabulary. Entities (pure domain objects), Use Cases (application orchestration), Interface Adapters (controllers and gateways), and Frameworks and Drivers (the actual database and web server). The dependency rule is unchanged: nothing from an outer ring may be named in an inner ring. Entities know nothing about use cases; use cases know nothing about HTTP.
words.longDefinition: Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob) published Clean Architecture: A Craftsman's Guide to Software Structure and Design in 2017, synthesizing hexagonal, onion, and several other layered approaches into a single diagram with four explicitly named rings. Entities are enterprise-wide business rules — aggregates, entities, and value objects in DDD terms. Use Cases are application-specific rules — the interactors that orchestrate entities. Interface Adapters convert data between the format of use cases and the format of external agencies (HTTP controllers, database gateways, presenters). Frameworks and Drivers are the outermost ring: Spring, Hibernate, React, PostgreSQL — details that the inner rings must never mention. Martin's diagram features a prominent arrow labeled 'DEPENDENCY RULE' pointing inward, and the canonical note: 'The name of something declared in an outer circle must not be mentioned by the code in an inner circle.' In DDD applications, Clean Architecture and Onion Architecture are structurally identical — the difference is primarily vocabulary and framing.
words.connector: Think of clean architecture like a government's chain of authority: the constitution (entities) sets the highest law, statutes (use cases) implement it, regulations (adapters) apply it, and enforcement agencies (frameworks) execute it — but no constitutional clause may be amended by a regulatory decision.
words.techContext: We adopted Clean Architecture's explicit Entities / Use Cases ring separation because it gave our junior developers a clear decision rule for where to place any new class — the interview answer was always 'which ring is it?'
words.exampleSentence: Clean Architecture's four-ring diagram gave our distributed team a shared mental model that survived two framework migrations and a database engine change with no rewrites to the Entity or Use Case rings.
words.etymology: Named by Robert C. Martin in his 2017 book; 'clean' signals the goal of code free of framework coupling, database coupling, and UI coupling — isolating what Martin calls 'the business rules.'

words.shortDefinition: The principle that a project's top-level folder structure should reveal the domain (e.g. /billing, /orders) not the framework.
words.simpleDefinition: Screaming architecture is Robert C. Martin's principle that a codebase's directory structure should announce what the system does before revealing how it is built. A project whose top-level folders are /controllers, /models, and /views screams 'Rails app.' A project whose top-level folders are /billing, /orders, /inventory, and /shipping screams 'e-commerce domain.' DDD practitioners adopt screaming architecture as a structural expression of the ubiquitous language.
words.longDefinition: Robert C. Martin coined 'screaming architecture' in a blog post, arguing that the first thing a developer should learn about a system from its folder structure is its purpose, not its framework. A directory tree that begins with /controllers, /services, /repositories, and /models reveals nothing about the domain — it could be any application in any industry. A directory tree that begins with /ordering, /billing, /inventory, and /fulfillment tells the reader immediately what the system does. In DDD, screaming architecture aligns naturally with bounded contexts: each top-level package corresponds to a bounded context, and the internal structure of each package may then reflect the hexagonal or onion layers. The practical benefit is onboarding speed — a developer new to the codebase finds the right package from domain knowledge, not from framework convention. The challenge is maintaining the structure as the system grows and context boundaries shift.
words.connector: Think of screaming architecture like the layout of a department store: the floor map screams 'menswear,' 'electronics,' 'sporting goods' — not 'fitting rooms,' 'registers,' 'stock rooms.' Shoppers navigate by purpose, not by store infrastructure.
words.techContext: After restructuring from a framework-first layout (/controllers, /services) to a domain-first layout (/billing, /orders, /catalog), onboarding new developers dropped from two weeks of orientation to three days.
words.exampleSentence: Screaming architecture made our bounded context map self-documenting — any developer could open the project root and immediately see the five contexts, their names matching the ubiquitous language exactly.

codeExample.code:
// Framework-first layout — says nothing about the domain
src/
  controllers/
  services/
  repositories/
  models/

// Screaming architecture — domain is the first thing visible
src/
  ordering/
    domain/
    application/
    infrastructure/
  billing/
    domain/
    application/
    infrastructure/
  inventory/
    domain/
    application/
    infrastructure/

words.etymology: Coined by Robert C. Martin; 'screaming' is intentionally dramatic — a well-structured architecture does not whisper its domain, it shouts it from the folder tree.

words.shortDefinition: An organization strategy grouping all layers of a feature together by use case rather than by technical layer.
words.simpleDefinition: Vertical slice architecture groups every layer a feature needs — its command, handler, validator, persistence query, and HTTP endpoint — into a single feature folder instead of scattering them across horizontal technical layers. Each slice is a self-contained unit of behavior. The alternative to organizing by technical layer (all controllers together, all repositories together), it pairs naturally with screaming architecture and minimizes cross-layer coupling.
words.longDefinition: Popularized by Jimmy Bogard and the MediatR community, vertical slice architecture organizes code around use cases rather than technical responsibilities. Instead of a /controllers folder containing all HTTP handlers, a /services folder containing all service classes, and a /repositories folder containing all database code, each use case gets its own folder containing everything it needs end-to-end: the request/response objects, the command handler, the validation logic, the database query, and sometimes the HTTP endpoint binding. In DDD terms, each slice corresponds to a single use case in the application service layer. The benefit is cohesion: changing a use case touches one folder instead of four. The challenge is shared logic — if two slices share domain rules, those rules should live in the domain model, not be duplicated across slices. Vertical slice architecture and hexagonal architecture are not mutually exclusive: slices can be organized within a hexagonal package structure.
words.connector: Think of vertical slicing like organizing a kitchen by meal rather than by utensil: instead of all knives in one drawer, all cutting boards in another, and all pans in a third, you have a 'steak dinner station' with everything needed for one meal in one place.
words.techContext: Each feature in our ordering service is a vertical slice: the PlaceOrder folder contains the command, handler, validator, event, and integration test — a developer can understand and change the entire feature without opening any other folder.
words.exampleSentence: Vertical slice architecture reduced our average PR size from 12 files across 4 layers to 4 files in a single feature folder, making code review dramatically faster and easier.

codeExample.code:
// Vertical slice organization — each use case is self-contained
ordering/
  PlaceOrder/
    PlaceOrderCommand.java
    PlaceOrderHandler.java      // application service
    PlaceOrderValidator.java
    PlaceOrderController.java   // driving adapter
    PlaceOrderHandlerTest.java
  CancelOrder/
    CancelOrderCommand.java
    CancelOrderHandler.java
    CancelOrderController.java
    CancelOrderHandlerTest.java
  // Shared domain model lives outside slices
  domain/
    Order.java
    OrderRepository.java

words.etymology: The 'vertical' contrasts with horizontal technical layers; a slice cuts through all layers for a single use case, taking a thin vertical column from top to bottom.

words.shortDefinition: Alberto Brandolini's collaborative workshop that uses sticky notes to discover domain events, commands, and aggregates rapidly.
words.simpleDefinition: Event Storming covers a long wall with paper and invites everyone who knows the business alongside everyone who will build the software. Participants write business events on orange sticky notes in past tense — Order Placed, Payment Failed, Shipment Dispatched — and arrange them on a timeline. The arguing about placement is the point: it surfaces domain disagreements in hours that would otherwise cause production bugs in months.
words.longDefinition: Alberto Brandolini invented Event Storming in 2013 and formalized it in his Leanpub book Introducing EventStorming (2017). The workshop fuses Domain Events — the core DDD concept of significant, past-tense business facts — with brainstorming. In a physical session, participants stand around a very long paper-covered wall, writing events on orange sticky notes and placing them chronologically. Commands (blue), aggregates (yellow), policies (lilac), and external systems (pink) are added progressively. The workshop is intentionally chaotic before it becomes structured: volume of stickies signals how much domain knowledge was previously implicit. Brandolini has called it 'the highest ROI activity in software development' because it surfaces naming conflicts, missing concepts, and bounded context boundaries in hours. The three zoom levels — big-picture (entire business), process-level (one workflow), and design-level (aggregates and invariants) — allow teams to start broad and drill into specifics. Virtual canvases (Miro, Mural, EventModeler) replicate the mechanics for remote teams.
words.connector: Think of Event Storming like a crime board the detective builds with string and photos: everyone adds what they know, connections emerge visually, and the board surfaces the pattern that no single person could have seen alone.
words.techContext: A three-hour big-picture Event Storming session with our e-commerce domain experts revealed four bounded context candidates and eleven hot spots — more than six weeks of requirements meetings had produced in the previous quarter.
words.exampleSentence: Event Storming surfaced a naming conflict that had gone undetected for two years: the sales team's 'contract' and the legal team's 'agreement' were the same concept, encoded differently in two microservices with a silent translation bug between them.
words.etymology: Coined by Alberto Brandolini by fusing 'Domain Event' (the DDD concept) with 'brainstorming'; the name signals deliberate chaos — storm first, structure later.

words.shortDefinition: The highest-level event storming format mapping the entire business flow to identify bounded contexts and pain points.
words.simpleDefinition: Big-picture event storming is the wide-angle scan: all stakeholders in one room (10–30 people), mapping the entire business on one very long wall. The goal is not a precise model but a shared landscape — what happens, where the pain lives, and where bounded contexts might form. Pivotal events that mark major state transitions become natural chapter breaks and often reveal context boundaries.
words.longDefinition: Big-picture event storming is the strategic level of Alberto Brandolini's three-format progression. It is run with the largest cross-functional group — domain experts from every part of the business, product managers, and engineers — and requires a minimum of 8 meters of uninterrupted wall space. The session proceeds through four phases: chaotic exploration (everyone writes orange stickies simultaneously), timeline ordering (the group arranges events chronologically, with disputes flagged as hot spots), hot spot marking (areas of confusion, disagreement, or missing knowledge), and opportunity identification (high-value events marked in green to connect domain modeling to product strategy). The output is not a domain model but a domain landscape: a shared picture of how the business works, where the complexity is concentrated, and which areas warrant deeper process-level exploration. Bounded context candidates emerge naturally as regions of the timeline with distinct vocabulary, cohesive aggregates, and clear pivotal event boundaries.
words.connector: Think of big-picture event storming like a satellite view of a city: you see districts, main roads, and concentrations of activity, but not individual buildings. It answers 'what is here?' before 'how does this work?'
words.techContext: Our two-day big-picture Event Storming with fifty participants mapped an eighteen-year-old monolith onto a timeline that revealed seven distinct bounded context candidates — the input to six months of strategic modernization work.
words.exampleSentence: Big-picture event storming with the entire product division produced a domain landscape in one day that aligned fifteen engineers, four product managers, and six domain experts on a context map that had never previously been made explicit.
words.etymology: The 'big picture' qualifier distinguishes this from the more detailed process-level and design-level formats; Brandolini uses the phrase to indicate maximum breadth at minimum depth.

words.shortDefinition: A mid-level event storming format that models a specific end-to-end business process in detail including commands and policies.
words.simpleDefinition: Process-level event storming zooms into one process identified during big-picture exploration. A smaller group (5–10 people) adds commands (blue) and the actors who issue them, policies (lilac) that fire automatically between events, and external system touchpoints (pink). The output is a detailed narrative of one workflow: who does what, what happens as a result, and where asynchronous automation kicks in — sufficient to define bounded context APIs and write user stories.
words.longDefinition: Process-level event storming is Brandolini's middle zoom level, sitting between the strategic width of big-picture and the aggregate precision of design-level. Once big-picture storming has identified a high-value or high-complexity process — often flagged by a cluster of hot spots — a process-level session focuses exclusively on that workflow with a smaller, more focused group. Blue command stickies are placed to the left of the events they cause, making causation explicit. Actor labels (customer, warehouse operator, automated service) are placed next to commands to make responsibility visible. Lilac policy stickies fill the gaps between events and the commands they trigger, making implicit automation explicit — 'when an order is placed, reserve inventory' is a policy. Pink external system stickies mark where a third-party service is involved, signaling an anticorruption layer boundary. The result maps directly to bounded context API contracts: events that cross context boundaries in the process-level model become the integration events that teams agree on before writing code.
words.connector: Think of process-level event storming like a theater director's table read: every line and cue is mapped in sequence, actors know their entrances and exits, and the director can see where a scene needs restructuring before anyone steps on stage.
words.techContext: A process-level event storming session between our Order and Inventory teams produced an agreed event contract — OrderPlaced triggering InventoryReservationRequested — that replaced a month of Slack debate about API shape.
words.exampleSentence: Process-level event storming for the returns workflow revealed three implicit policies that had been implemented inconsistently across four services, producing the first documented view of how a return actually worked end-to-end.
words.etymology: The 'process-level' qualifier signals that this format models a specific business process rather than the entire domain landscape (big-picture) or the internal aggregate design (design-level).

words.shortDefinition: An immutable, past-tense fact recorded within one bounded context signaling something meaningful occurred in the domain.
words.simpleDefinition: A domain event is a record of something that happened in the domain that the business cares about — OrderPlaced, PaymentFailed, AccountSuspended. It is written in past tense because it is a fact: it already happened and cannot be rejected. Domain events carry just enough information for handlers to act on them, use the ubiquitous language, and are raised by aggregate roots as the primary mechanism for signaling state changes.
words.longDefinition: Vaughn Vernon defines a domain event as 'something that happened in the domain that domain experts care about.' The definition has two requirements: the event must have already happened (it is immutable and past-tense) and it must matter to the business (not every state change warrants an event). Domain events are raised by aggregate roots during command processing: when an Order aggregate confirms a purchase, it raises an OrderPlaced event rather than calling downstream services directly. This decouples the aggregate from its consumers. Within a bounded context, domain events drive reactive behavior via policies: the 'whenever an order is placed, reserve inventory' rule is an event handler that listens for OrderPlaced. At context boundaries, domain events become integration events — translated and published to a message broker for other contexts to consume. In event-sourced systems, domain events become the primary storage format: the aggregate's current state is derived by replaying its event stream.
words.connector: Think of a domain event like an entry in a ship's log: each entry records what happened, when, and the relevant details — it is a fact, already past, and the record itself cannot be undone even if the ship later changes course.
words.techContext: Every aggregate root in our system raises domain events instead of calling other services directly — the OrderPlaced event is consumed by three handlers: inventory reservation, payment initiation, and email notification.
words.exampleSentence: Switching from direct service calls to domain events reduced the Order aggregate's dependency list from seven injected services to zero — it only raised events, and the application layer wired the handlers.
words.etymology: From 'domain' (the bounded area of business knowledge) + 'event' (Latin eventus: an outcome or occurrence); popularized by Vaughn Vernon in Implementing Domain-Driven Design (2013).

words.shortDefinition: Command Query Responsibility Segregation — separating the write model (commands) from the read model (queries) in a bounded context.
words.simpleDefinition: CQRS splits every operation into exactly two kinds: commands (write, change state, no return data) and queries (read, return data, no side effects). The write model — aggregates, domain events, invariant enforcement — is optimized for correctness. The read model — projections, denormalized views, read-optimized stores — is optimized for query performance. Commands go through aggregates; queries bypass them entirely.
words.longDefinition: Command Query Responsibility Segregation was formalized by Greg Young and Udi Dahan around 2009, building on Bertrand Meyer's Command Query Separation principle. In a DDD bounded context, CQRS recognizes that the aggregate model — rich with invariant enforcement and domain logic — is excellent for processing commands but a poor fit for complex queries that need to join multiple aggregates or denormalize data for a UI. The write side uses the full DDD tactical pattern: aggregates enforce invariants, raise domain events, and are persisted via repositories. The read side uses projections — materialized views built by consuming the domain event stream — that are optimized for specific query shapes. Queries target the read model directly, bypassing aggregates entirely. This removes the impedance mismatch between a rich domain model and a flat query result. CQRS does not mandate separate databases: a simple implementation uses a single database with separate read tables built by event handlers. Complex implementations use separate stores (PostgreSQL for writes, Elasticsearch for reads) with eventual consistency between them.
words.connector: Think of CQRS like a restaurant with a kitchen (write side) and a menu (read side): the kitchen enforces food safety rules and executes the cooking; the menu presents the results in a format optimized for customers, not for the kitchen's internal organization.
words.techContext: After applying CQRS to our Order context, the dashboard query that previously joined seven aggregate tables became a direct read from a pre-projected order-summary table updated by domain event handlers.
words.exampleSentence: CQRS eliminated the N+1 query problem in our Order list view — the read model projection was updated by event handlers the moment an OrderPlaced event fired, so the query became a single SELECT from a denormalized table.
words.etymology: Coined by Greg Young circa 2009; expands Bertrand Meyer's Command Query Separation (CQS) principle from the method level to the architectural level of entire models.

words.shortDefinition: Persisting aggregate state as an append-only log of domain events, reconstructing current state by replaying them.
words.simpleDefinition: Event sourcing stores every state change as a domain event appended to a log, rather than overwriting the current state in a row. To find out what an aggregate looks like now, replay all its events from the beginning. To find out what it looked like last Tuesday, replay events up to Tuesday. The audit trail is not a separate feature — it is the primary data model.
words.longDefinition: Event sourcing is a persistence strategy where aggregate state is never updated in place. Every command that changes an aggregate produces one or more domain events that are appended to an event store — an immutable, ordered log. To reconstitute an aggregate, the repository loads the event stream for that aggregate ID and replays each event in sequence, applying it to rebuild state. This eliminates the ORM impedance mismatch between rich domain objects and flat database rows: the event store stores events, not object state, so the aggregate is free to evolve its internal structure without database migrations. The business benefits include a complete, immutable audit trail; the ability to reconstruct state at any point in time; and the ability to build new read models (projections) from historical events. The engineering challenges include event schema evolution (old events must be readable by new code), growing event streams (mitigated by snapshots), and the mental shift away from CRUD. Event sourcing pairs naturally with CQRS: the write side produces events, and the read side builds projections from them.
words.connector: Think of event sourcing like a double-entry ledger in accounting: rather than updating a balance column, every transaction is recorded as a new line. The current balance is always computable by summing all the lines — and the full history is never lost.
words.techContext: Adopting event sourcing for our Payment aggregate gave us a forensic audit trail that resolved a disputed charge in minutes — we replayed the event stream and saw exactly when and why the charge state transitioned.
words.exampleSentence: Event sourcing let us build a new fraud-detection read model retroactively by replaying two years of OrderPlaced events through a new projection handler without touching the production write side at all.
words.etymology: The term 'event sourcing' was popularized by Greg Young and Martin Fowler around 2005–2010; 'sourcing' refers to the events being the source of truth from which current state is derived.

words.shortDefinition: The combined pattern pairing event sourcing for the write side with separate read-optimized projections, popular with DDD aggregates.
words.simpleDefinition: CQRS + Event Sourcing is the combined pattern where commands go through DDD aggregates that persist state as domain events (write side), and queries read from projections built by consuming those events (read side). The aggregate is the event-producing, invariant-enforcing write model. The projection is the query-optimized read model. Domain events are the bridge: produced by the write side and consumed by the read side to keep projections current.
words.longDefinition: When CQRS and event sourcing are combined with DDD aggregates, each pattern reinforces the others. DDD provides the aggregate as the consistency boundary and the domain event as the meaningful fact. Event sourcing makes the aggregate's history the primary store, eliminating ORM friction and providing a full audit trail. CQRS uses the same event stream to build read-optimized projections, removing the impedance between a rich domain model and flat query results. The flow is: a command arrives at an application service, which loads the aggregate by replaying its event stream, calls the domain method, persists new events to the event store, and publishes those events to a projection handler that updates the read model. Queries target the read model directly. This combination is popular for financial systems, e-commerce order management, and any domain where auditability and complex query shapes both matter. The tradeoff is operational complexity: event schema evolution, projection rebuilds, and eventual consistency between write and read sides require disciplined engineering.
words.connector: Think of CQRS + ES + DDD like a live sports scoreboard: a referee (aggregate) enforces the rules and records each score as a fact (event); a scoreboard operator (projection handler) reads those facts and updates the display (read model) viewers see.
words.techContext: Our Payment context uses CQRS + ES with DDD: every command goes through the Payment aggregate, which appends events to EventStoreDB; three projections consume those events to serve the billing dashboard, the fraud API, and the customer statement view.
words.exampleSentence: The CQRS + ES combination let us rebuild our customer statement projection from scratch in 40 minutes by replaying three years of PaymentProcessed events — no data migration, no downtime, no changes to the write side.
words.etymology: A compound abbreviation formed from CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation, Greg Young 2009) + ES (Event Sourcing, popularized 2005–2010) applied within the DDD tactical pattern set.

words.shortDefinition: A migration strategy that incrementally replaces a legacy system by routing traffic through a new system until the old one is gone.
words.simpleDefinition: The strangler fig pattern gradually replaces a legacy monolith by intercepting requests at a facade and routing them — piece by piece — to new services. The legacy system handles everything at first. Over time, new bounded contexts handle more and more routes. The legacy system shrinks as the new system grows around it. When all routes are migrated, the legacy system is removed and only the new system remains.
words.longDefinition: Martin Fowler coined the strangler fig pattern in 2004, named after a tropical plant that grows around a host tree, gradually taking over its structure until the original tree dies and only the fig remains. In software, a facade (reverse proxy, API gateway, or routing layer) sits in front of both the legacy system and the new system. Initially, all traffic passes through to the legacy. As new bounded contexts are built using DDD tactical patterns, the facade begins routing specific paths to the new system. Each migration step is independently deployable: the legacy is not modified, the new service handles a defined set of operations, and the routing rule is adjusted. This approach eliminates the 'big bang' rewrite risk. The challenge in a DDD migration is identifying the right bounded context boundaries to extract — poor boundaries produce a distributed monolith instead of a clean context map. The anticorruption layer (ACL) is the companion pattern: during coexistence, the new bounded context uses an ACL to translate the legacy system's model into the new context's ubiquitous language.
words.connector: Think of the strangler fig pattern like remodeling a house while living in it: you rebuild room by room, routing your daily life through the finished rooms while demolishing the old ones, until the original structure is entirely gone and only the new construction remains.
words.techContext: We used the strangler fig pattern to extract the Billing bounded context from a fifteen-year-old PHP monolith — the API gateway routed /billing/* to the new service six months after we started, with the monolith still handling everything else.
words.exampleSentence: The strangler fig pattern let us decommission the legacy order management system over eighteen months with zero downtime — each sprint migrated one more operation to the new Order bounded context while the monolith kept the rest running.

codeExample.code:
# API Gateway routing — strangler fig routing table
# Traffic migrated progressively from legacy to new services
routes:
  - path: /orders/*
    methods: [POST]
    target: new-order-service      # migrated
  - path: /orders/*
    methods: [GET]
    target: new-order-service      # migrated
  - path: /inventory/*
    target: legacy-monolith        # not yet migrated
  - path: /billing/*
    target: new-billing-service    # migrated
  - path: /shipping/*
    target: legacy-monolith        # scheduled for Q3

words.etymology: Named by Martin Fowler in 2004 after the strangler fig (Ficus species) — a tropical plant that germinates in a host tree's canopy, grows roots downward, and eventually kills the host by surrounding and replacing its trunk.

words.shortDefinition: Combining strangler fig migration with an anticorruption layer to keep the new domain model clean during legacy coexistence.
words.simpleDefinition: When a new DDD bounded context coexists with a legacy system during a strangler fig migration, the legacy system's data model leaks into the new context unless something stops it. An anticorruption layer (ACL) is that barrier: it sits at the seam between old and new, translating the legacy system's concepts into the new bounded context's ubiquitous language. The ACL ensures the new model is designed around the real domain, not around the legacy data model's accidents.
words.longDefinition: The strangler fig pattern manages deployment topology — gradually shifting traffic from legacy to new. The anticorruption layer manages model integrity — ensuring the new bounded context's model is not corrupted by the legacy system's vocabulary and structure. During coexistence, the new service frequently needs data from the legacy system: it may call the legacy API, read from the legacy database, or consume the legacy message queue. Without an ACL, the new service's domain model gets shaped by legacy field names, legacy status codes, and legacy data structures. The ACL is the translation layer that converts legacy representations into the new context's own types. For example, if the legacy system uses numeric status codes (1 = confirmed, 2 = shipped) and the new Order context uses OrderStatus.CONFIRMED and OrderStatus.SHIPPED, the ACL translates on the boundary. As the migration progresses and the legacy system shrinks, ACL code is progressively simplified and eventually removed when the legacy source disappears. The Strangler Fig + ACL combination is the DDD-idiomatic approach to legacy modernization: migrate incrementally and translate at the boundary.
words.connector: Think of Strangler Fig + ACL like an embassy's interpreter: the new country (bounded context) coexists alongside the old regime (legacy), and the interpreter (ACL) translates every communication so that the new country's officials never need to learn the old regime's jargon.
words.techContext: Our ACL translated the legacy billing system's 14 numeric invoice states into our new Invoice aggregate's three domain states, ensuring the new model's ubiquitous language was never contaminated by legacy data oddities.
words.exampleSentence: Without the ACL, the legacy system's concept of a 'pending_review' status — a historical artifact of a 2008 compliance requirement — would have infected our new billing model and required us to maintain that concept indefinitely.
words.etymology: A compound of two established DDD/architecture patterns: Strangler Fig Pattern (Martin Fowler, 2004) and Anticorruption Layer (Eric Evans, DDD Blue Book, 2003).

words.shortDefinition: A single-deployment application with strong internal module boundaries matching bounded contexts, avoiding microservice overhead.
words.simpleDefinition: A modular monolith deploys as one unit but is internally structured with the same discipline as a microservice system: each bounded context is a distinct module with its own domain model, database schema (or schema namespace), and public API — but all modules run in the same process. Modules communicate through well-defined interfaces, not by sharing classes or databases. The result is microservice-level coupling discipline without microservice-level operational complexity.
words.longDefinition: The modular monolith is the DDD-idiomatic starting architecture for most systems and the recommended migration target for teams extracting bounded contexts from a big ball of mud. In a modular monolith, each bounded context is a first-class code module with its own package boundary, its own aggregate roots, its own repository implementations, and its own database schema (implemented as schema namespaces or separate schema prefixes in one database). Modules communicate with each other only through their public application service interfaces — no cross-module direct repository calls, no shared domain objects. Domain events published in one module are consumed by other modules through an in-process event bus, providing the same decoupling as a message broker without the operational overhead of Kafka or RabbitMQ. The architectural benefit over microservices is that cross-cutting concerns — transactions, debugging, distributed tracing, service discovery, network failure handling — are all simpler in a single process. The benefit over a traditional monolith is that the internal structure makes bounded context boundaries clear and enforceable by build tooling. Teams frequently start with a modular monolith and extract specific modules into independent services only when an individual bounded context has a scaling or deployment requirement that justifies the operational overhead.
words.connector: Think of a modular monolith like a well-organized open-plan office: everyone is in the same building (process), but each team has its own designated area and communicates through defined channels rather than wandering through each other's desks.
words.techContext: We built our platform as a modular monolith with six bounded context modules sharing one PostgreSQL database via schema prefixes — we have been running it in production for two years and extracted only the Search module as a separate service when full-text indexing required Elasticsearch.
words.exampleSentence: The modular monolith gave us bounded context discipline from day one and deferred the operational complexity of microservices until two specific modules genuinely needed independent scaling — eighteen months after launch.

codeExample.code:
// Modular monolith structure — each module is a bounded context
src/
  ordering/           // BC: Ordering
    domain/
    application/
    infrastructure/
    OrderingModule.java     // public API of this module
  billing/            // BC: Billing
    domain/
    application/
    infrastructure/
    BillingModule.java
  inventory/          // BC: Inventory
    ...

// Cross-module communication via events or public module API only
// FORBIDDEN: billing.infrastructure.OrderRepository (cross-module DB access)
// ALLOWED:   ordering.OrderingModule.getOrder(orderId)  (public API)

words.etymology: A compound of 'modular' (composed of distinct modules with defined interfaces) + 'monolith' (deployed as a single unit); the term gained prominence in the 2018–2022 period as a reaction to microservice complexity.

words.shortDefinition: Over-decomposition of microservices to one aggregate per service, creating excessive inter-service coordination overhead.
words.simpleDefinition: The nano-service anti-pattern emerges when teams take microservice decomposition too far: one aggregate per service, or even one entity per service. The resulting services are too fine-grained to maintain bounded context integrity. What should be one atomic business operation now requires coordinating multiple services across network calls, distributed transactions, or sagas — adding complexity without any of the autonomy benefits that motivated microservices.
words.longDefinition: The nano-service anti-pattern is the mirror image of the distributed monolith. Where a distributed monolith cuts services too coarsely (one service that contains multiple bounded contexts and is accessed by all others), nano-services cut too finely (one service per aggregate or entity). The result is a system where a single business operation — placing an order — requires HTTP calls to an Order service, a Customer service, an Inventory service, a Pricing service, and a Promotion service. Each call can fail independently, creating distributed transaction problems. Sagas must be implemented to maintain eventual consistency, adding significant complexity. The cure for a nano-service system is DDD strategic design: identify the bounded contexts, which are the correct unit of service decomposition. Within a bounded context, multiple aggregates should coexist in a single service or module. The heuristic is that services should be sized to match bounded contexts — not to match individual aggregates, database tables, or team subgroups. Nano-services are often a symptom of applying microservice decomposition without domain analysis, producing 'micro' in name and 'nano' in practice.
words.connector: Think of nano-services like organizing a restaurant by ingredient: one station for salt, one for pepper, one for each vegetable. Every dish requires coordinating dozens of stations where five stations would suffice — the granularity is below the natural unit of work.
words.techContext: Our audit found seven services that together implemented the Order placement workflow — all in the same bounded context, all owned by one team — and merged them into a single service with one shared domain model and no inter-service coordination.
words.exampleSentence: The nano-service architecture required a ten-hop distributed call chain to place a single order, with six potential failure points that the team was managing through a custom saga orchestrator costing more effort than the services themselves.
words.etymology: A compound of 'nano' (prefix meaning 10⁻⁹, implying extremely small scale) + 'service' + 'anti-pattern'; the term emerged in the DDD and microservices community as a counterpoint to the naïve 'smaller is always better' heuristic.

words.shortDefinition: The practice of sizing microservices to bounded context boundaries rather than technical layers or entity types.
words.simpleDefinition: A domain-aligned service boundary places the fence around a microservice where the domain model changes — at the bounded context boundary — not where the database table ends or the team subgroup starts. One bounded context per service (at most). The service owns its ubiquitous language, its data, and its deployment pipeline. No other service reads its database; no shared domain objects cross the wire.
words.longDefinition: Domain-aligned service boundaries apply DDD's bounded context concept as the primary heuristic for microservice decomposition. The insight — articulated by Sam Newman, Vaughn Vernon, and the DDD community — is that the natural service boundary is the boundary of model coherence: the scope within which a term like 'Order' or 'Customer' has a single, agreed-upon meaning. Cutting a service boundary through the middle of a bounded context produces two services that share a domain model, creating coupling. Cutting a service boundary that encompasses two bounded contexts produces one service carrying two models and the friction between them. A domain-aligned service boundary therefore: encompasses all aggregates and domain services belonging to one bounded context; owns its own database schema exclusively; exposes its capabilities via a versioned API using the bounded context's ubiquitous language; and publishes integration events when significant domain events occur within the context. This sizing means services are often larger than nano-services but smaller than a full monolith. The team structure aligns: one team owns one bounded context service, matching the inverse Conway manoeuvre.
words.connector: Think of a domain-aligned service boundary like a nation-state's border: drawn to reflect cultural and linguistic coherence rather than following geographic lines arbitrarily — the border is where the language and customs change, not where the mountains happen to be.
words.techContext: After redrawing our service boundaries around bounded contexts instead of database tables, we reduced our service count from 34 nano-services to 9 domain-aligned services and eliminated 80% of the inter-service calls.
words.exampleSentence: Domain-aligned service boundaries gave our platform teams clear ownership semantics: if you could name the bounded context, you could name the team that owned it, the service that implemented it, and the database schema that stored it.
words.etymology: Composite term from 'domain' (DDD's bounded context), 'aligned' (in correspondence with), and 'service boundary' (the deployment and ownership perimeter of a microservice); popularized in the DDD + microservices literature of the 2015–2020 period.

words.shortDefinition: Using LLMs to accelerate knowledge-crunching sessions — generating candidate event catalogs, aggregate drafts, and glossary entries.
words.simpleDefinition: AI-assisted domain modeling uses large language models as a first-pass domain analyst during knowledge-crunching sessions. Given a business description or interview transcript, an LLM can generate candidate event catalogs, propose aggregate boundaries, draft glossary entries, and flag naming inconsistencies. The model accelerates the early stages of DDD modeling but requires domain expert validation — LLMs hallucinate plausible-sounding but incorrect domain rules and cannot substitute for the collaborative discovery that makes the ubiquitous language real.
words.longDefinition: By 2025–2026, many DDD teams use LLMs as a structuring aid during the knowledge-crunching phase. The typical workflow: a domain expert is interviewed, the transcript is fed to an LLM, and the model outputs candidate domain event lists, proposed aggregates, suggested ubiquitous language terms, and cross-reference inconsistencies. This accelerates the time from 'first conversation' to 'first Event Storming session' from weeks to hours. LLMs are particularly useful for spotting naming inconsistencies in large text corpora (e.g., 'the business requirements say invoice, the API says bill, the UI says statement — are these the same?'), for generating a starting glossary that domain experts then validate and correct, and for proposing event names for review. The limitations are significant: LLMs cannot identify when a domain expert's statement is wrong or culturally constrained; they produce plausible-sounding aggregate designs that may violate real invariants; and they cannot run an Event Storming workshop — the social process of collaborative discovery is irreducible. AI-assisted domain modeling is best understood as a preprocessing accelerator, not a substitute for knowledge crunching with real experts.
words.connector: Think of AI-assisted domain modeling like having a research assistant who reads all your interview notes and prepares a first draft before the workshop: it saves the starting-from-blank-page overhead, but every entry must be validated by the people who actually know the domain.
words.techContext: We used an LLM to process 40 hours of stakeholder interview recordings and produce a candidate event catalog with 89 events — the Event Storming session then validated, merged, and corrected the list, keeping 61 and adding 14 that the LLM had missed.
words.exampleSentence: AI-assisted domain modeling cut our pre-workshop preparation from three weeks to two days, but the workshop itself remained unchanged — domain experts are irreplaceable for validating whether the candidate aggregates reflect the real business rules.
words.etymology: A compound of 'AI-assisted' (using artificial intelligence tools as an aid, not a replacement) and 'domain modeling' (the DDD practice of discovering and encoding the business model in software); the phrase emerged as LLM tooling matured in 2024–2026.

words.shortDefinition: A read-optimized view built by consuming a stream of domain events, used in CQRS to serve queries without hitting the write model.
words.simpleDefinition: A projection is a materialized view of domain state built by processing domain events one by one and updating a dedicated read store. When an OrderPlaced event fires, the order-summary projection handler inserts a row in the order_summary table. When an OrderCancelled event fires, it updates that row. Queries read from the projection — a simple, flat, query-optimized table — without ever touching the aggregate or its event log.
words.longDefinition: Projections are the read side of CQRS and the primary consumer of event-sourced streams. A projection is built by registering handlers for specific domain event types and maintaining a separate read store that is updated incrementally as events arrive. The read store can be any technology optimized for the query pattern: PostgreSQL tables for structured queries, Elasticsearch for full-text search, Redis for key-value lookups, or a graph database for relationship queries. Multiple projections can consume the same event stream, each building a different view optimized for a different query. Projections are eventually consistent with the write side: there is a window between when an event is persisted and when the projection is updated. In practice, this window is typically milliseconds. A key property of projections is rebuildability: since the event stream is immutable and append-only, a projection can be rebuilt from scratch at any time by replaying the entire event history through the projection handler. This makes projection schema migrations trivial — build the new projection from the event stream in parallel, then switch queries to it when complete.
words.connector: Think of a projection like a banking app's transaction history screen: it is not the ledger (write model) — it is a view built from ledger entries, formatted for quick reading, and updated each time a new transaction is recorded.
words.techContext: We maintain five projections from the Order event stream: order-summary (for the dashboard), order-detail (for the order page), customer-order-history (for the profile page), fraud-signals (for the risk engine), and order-fulfillment-status (for the warehouse app).
words.exampleSentence: When we added a new field to the order-summary projection, we rebuilt it from three years of event history in 22 minutes while the existing projection continued serving queries — then switched the query endpoint with no downtime.
words.etymology: From Latin projectio (a throwing forward); in mathematics, a projection maps a higher-dimensional structure onto a lower-dimensional one — similarly, a CQRS projection maps a rich event stream onto a flattened, query-optimized view.

words.shortDefinition: Rebuilding an aggregate's current state by replaying all its stored domain events from the beginning of its event log.
words.simpleDefinition: Aggregate reconstitution is the event sourcing mechanism for loading an aggregate. Instead of reading a current-state row from a database, the repository loads the aggregate's full event stream and replays each event through the aggregate's apply() methods in sequence. After replaying all events, the aggregate's in-memory state reflects its current state exactly. This is how event-sourced aggregates are loaded for every command that modifies them.
words.longDefinition: In an event-sourced system, aggregates are never stored as mutable state. The event store holds an ordered stream of domain events per aggregate ID. When an application service needs to load an aggregate to process a command, the repository retrieves all events for that aggregate from the event store and passes them to the aggregate's reconstitution logic. The aggregate applies each event in sequence — calling the matching apply(EventType) method — rebuilding its internal state without raising new events. The resulting in-memory aggregate reflects current state precisely. Once reconstituted, the aggregate can process a command and raise new events, which are appended to the event store. The reconstitution overhead — replaying all events every time — is acceptable for short event streams but becomes expensive for long-lived aggregates. The snapshot pattern (storing a periodic state checkpoint) mitigates this: the repository loads the latest snapshot and replays only events that occurred after it. Reconstitution is both a performance consideration and a correctness guarantee: because all state derives from the event log, reconstitution always produces the same result given the same events.
words.connector: Think of aggregate reconstitution like reconstructing what a bank account balance should be: rather than reading a 'current balance' field, you replay every deposit and withdrawal transaction from account opening to now — the balance emerges correctly from the history.
words.techContext: Our Order aggregate event streams average 12 events — reconstitution takes under 5 ms. For Customer aggregates averaging 340 events, we introduced snapshots that brought reconstitution time from 80 ms to under 3 ms.
words.exampleSentence: Aggregate reconstitution revealed a subtle bug in our legacy system: an Order aggregate with 200 events reconstituted to a state that differed from the state stored in the old CRUD table, exposing corrupted data we had never previously detected.
words.etymology: From Latin reconstituere (to restore or reconstitute); in event sourcing, the aggregate is reconstituted — its identity and state restored — from its historical record of events.

words.shortDefinition: An optimization for event sourcing that saves a periodic aggregate state checkpoint to avoid replaying the full event log.
words.simpleDefinition: The snapshot pattern solves the performance problem of event-sourced aggregates with long event histories. Instead of replaying every event from the beginning of time, the system periodically saves the aggregate's current state as a snapshot. When loading the aggregate next time, the repository loads the latest snapshot and replays only the events that occurred after it — a much smaller set. The event log remains the source of truth; the snapshot is an optimization artifact.
words.longDefinition: In event-sourced systems, aggregate reconstitution is efficient for short event streams but expensive for long-lived aggregates. A customer aggregate with five years of activity might have thousands of events; replaying them all on every command adds unacceptable latency. The snapshot pattern solves this by periodically capturing a serialized representation of the aggregate's current state — the snapshot — alongside the sequence number of the last event it reflects. When loading the aggregate, the repository checks for a snapshot: if one exists, it deserializes it and replays only events with a sequence number higher than the snapshot. The snapshot is stored in the event store or a separate snapshot store. Snapshot frequency is a tradeoff: snapshots after every 50 events provide near-constant load time at the cost of snapshot storage; snapshots after every 500 events reduce storage but increase worst-case load time. A key discipline is that snapshots are never the source of truth — they are a cache of the event replay result. If a snapshot is corrupted or missing, reconstitution from the full event stream must always produce the same result. This means the snapshot serialization format must be versioned carefully alongside the aggregate code.
words.connector: Think of the snapshot pattern like using a bookmark in a long book: instead of re-reading from page 1 every time, you place a bookmark at your current page and start reading from there next time — the full book is still there if the bookmark falls out.
words.techContext: We take snapshots every 100 events for our Customer aggregate — the most active aggregate in our system. This keeps reconstitution under 5 ms even for customers with 10,000+ lifetime events, while using only 2% more storage.
words.exampleSentence: After introducing snapshots for our Payment aggregate, the 95th percentile reconstitution time dropped from 340 ms to 8 ms — the difference between a user-noticeable delay and an imperceptible one.
words.etymology: The 'snapshot' metaphor refers to a photograph — a point-in-time capture of state — borrowed from database terminology where snapshot isolation describes a similar concept of capturing consistent state at a moment in time.

words.shortDefinition: A reactive business rule in event storming (lilac sticky) that fires a command whenever a specific domain event occurs.
words.simpleDefinition: A policy in event storming is a lilac sticky note that encodes a reactive business rule: 'Whenever [Event], then [Command].' Policies are the automation layer — the 'if this then that' logic that makes business processes self-driving. They sit between the event that triggers them and the command they produce, making implicit automation explicit on the timeline. At the code level, policies become event handlers, sagas, or process managers in the application layer.
words.longDefinition: Brandolini introduced policies in Event Storming as the mechanism for capturing reactive business rules that are often buried in code or tribal knowledge. A policy is a statement of the form 'whenever [domain event] occurs, [command] must be issued.' For example: 'Whenever a Payment Fails, send a failure notification to the customer.' 'Whenever an Order is Placed, reserve inventory.' 'Whenever inventory drops below the reorder threshold, raise a purchase order.' In the event storming notation, lilac stickies are placed between the orange event that triggers the policy and the blue command the policy fires. Policies make automation visible to domain experts — in requirements meetings, experts often say 'oh, and when that happens, we also automatically...' which is exactly the cue for a policy sticky. Policies that cross bounded context boundaries are integration points: 'Whenever an Order is Placed in the Sales context, the Inventory context must Reserve Stock' signals an asynchronous cross-context event that needs careful API design. At the implementation level, a policy becomes an event handler in the application layer that subscribes to a domain event and issues a command — either directly within the same context or via a message broker to another context.
words.connector: Think of a policy like an 'if this, then that' automation rule: the trigger is a business event, the action is a business command, and the policy makes the causal chain visible and agreed upon before any code is written.
words.techContext: Event storming revealed eleven policies in our order fulfillment flow — six were already implemented, two were implemented incorrectly (as synchronous calls where the policy clearly implied asynchronous), and three had never been implemented at all.
words.exampleSentence: Making the 'whenever a payment fails, retry after one hour' logic explicit as a policy in event storming revealed that three different teams had each implemented their own version of this rule with different retry counts and backoff strategies.
words.etymology: From Latin politia (governance or administration); in event storming, a policy governs the automatic response to a domain event — the rule that runs without human decision at that moment.

words.shortDefinition: A red sticky placed in event storming to flag a conflict, ambiguity, or area of high disagreement requiring deeper discussion.
words.simpleDefinition: A hotspot in event storming is an honest 'we don't know' stuck to the wall in public. It marks any area where the model is wrong, incomplete, contested, or simply unknown: a term that means different things to different participants, a business rule that experts disagree on, a section of the timeline no one can explain confidently, or a decision that needs stakeholders not in the room. Hotspots are captured, not solved during the session, to maintain momentum.
words.longDefinition: Brandolini designed hotspots to solve a recurring problem in requirements workshops: unresolved questions derail the meeting. In traditional sessions, a disputed business rule becomes a 30-minute debate that halts progress and exhausts participants. Event Storming's hotspot mechanism breaks this pattern: when a dispute arises, a pink or red sticky is placed on the model at that point, the team acknowledges that this is unresolved, and the session moves on. The hotspot accumulates the question but defers the answer. Common hotspot triggers: naming conflicts (the sales team says 'contract,' the legal team says 'agreement' — both are on the wall, both are right in their context, and the hotspot flags a bounded context boundary candidate); missing domain experts (a section of the timeline where no one in the room can confidently explain the business rules); invariant disagreements (two experts give opposite answers to 'can an order be cancelled after it has shipped?'); and complexity flags (a region with dense causality that needs its own process-level session). After the event storming session, hotspots are triaged: decisions needed (requires a business owner to decide), follow-up sessions required (needs a deeper process-level exploration), and accepted risks (understood but deferred). Hotspots are the agenda for post-workshop domain modeling work.
words.connector: Think of a hotspot like a Post-it note on a map that says 'HERE THERE BE DRAGONS' — it does not solve the problem, but it makes sure the problem is not invisible and will not be accidentally ignored by the next navigator.
words.techContext: Our big-picture event storming session produced 23 hotspots. Six were naming conflicts that revealed bounded context boundaries. Four required missing domain experts to be invited to follow-up sessions. Three became explicit architectural risk items in our roadmap.
words.exampleSentence: The hotspot that asked 'who owns the customer lifecycle — Sales or CRM?' sat on the wall for six months as a placeholder for a cross-team decision that, once made, dictated the ownership of an entire bounded context.
words.etymology: The term 'hotspot' originally referred to areas of high radioactivity or high network activity — in event storming it marks areas of high conceptual heat: where the most disagreement or uncertainty is concentrated.

words.shortDefinition: The alignment of Skelton and Pais's stream-aligned team pattern with DDD's one-team-per-bounded-context principle.
words.simpleDefinition: Team Topologies (Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, 2019) provides four team types: stream-aligned, enabling, complicated-subsystem, and platform. DDD's inverse Conway manoeuvre says structure teams to match the desired architecture. The alignment: each stream-aligned team owns one bounded context end-to-end — its domain model, its service, its data, its deployment. This maps Conway's Law from a risk into a design tool, ensuring system architecture and team structure reinforce each other.
words.longDefinition: Team Topologies introduced a vocabulary for intentional team structure design in 2019. The stream-aligned team is the primary team type — a cross-functional team aligned to a single stream of business value. DDD's bounded context is the natural unit of business value in a domain-modeled system. The alignment is direct: one stream-aligned team owns one bounded context. The team owns the ubiquitous language, the aggregate model, the service implementation, the database, and the deployment pipeline. No other team modifies the bounded context's internals. This realises the inverse Conway manoeuvre: by structuring teams around bounded context boundaries, the system architecture naturally matches those boundaries because Conway's Law works in your favor. Enabling teams provide temporary capability uplift (helping a stream-aligned team adopt event sourcing, for example) and then move on. Complicated-subsystem teams own technical components that are too complex for a single stream-aligned team (a shared event store, a specialized ML model). Platform teams provide self-service infrastructure that all stream-aligned teams consume. The Team Topologies + DDD pairing also resolves the ownership of the context map: each edge on the context map between two bounded contexts is the interface between two stream-aligned teams, and the context-map relationship (customer-supplier, partnership, conformist) defines the inter-team working mode.
words.connector: Think of Team Topologies + DDD like a sports league structure: each team (stream-aligned) owns a stadium (bounded context) and plays on its own field. The league office (platform team) provides shared infrastructure. Coaches (enabling teams) help teams improve and move on.
words.techContext: Restructuring from functional teams (backend team, frontend team, data team) to stream-aligned teams aligned to bounded contexts reduced our average PR review wait from 4 days to 6 hours — the team reviewing the code owned the domain.
words.exampleSentence: Mapping our six bounded contexts to six stream-aligned teams using Team Topologies resolved three years of cross-team ownership disputes — each hotspot on our context map had a clear inter-team working mode rather than an ambiguous shared responsibility.
words.etymology: A compound reference to Team Topologies (Skelton and Pais, 2019) and Domain-Driven Design (Evans, 2003); the pairing was popularized by Nick Tune, Eduardo da Silva, and others in the DDD community from 2020 onward.

words.shortDefinition: Using an anticorruption layer as a seam to incrementally modernize a legacy system without disrupting the new domain model.
words.simpleDefinition: A legacy ACL migration places an anticorruption layer at the boundary between a new DDD bounded context and the legacy system it is replacing or consuming. The ACL acts as a seam that translates legacy concepts into the new ubiquitous language, insulating the new model from the legacy system's data accidents. As the migration progresses and the legacy shrinks, the ACL code progressively simplifies until it is removed entirely.
words.longDefinition: Legacy ACL migration is the DDD-idiomatic lifecycle of an anticorruption layer during a system modernization. In the early phase, the ACL is thick: the legacy system has many concepts, data formats, and naming conventions that must be translated into the new bounded context's model. The ACL may consume a legacy REST API, query a legacy database directly, or translate messages from a legacy message bus. The new bounded context's domain model is designed around the real domain — how the business actually works — not around the legacy system's data model, which reflects historical implementation accidents. As the strangler fig migration progresses and the legacy system handles fewer operations, the ACL's translation surface shrinks. Interfaces that were thick (converting 14 legacy status codes into 3 domain states) become thinner (the legacy system now only has 3 states).
